scenario: Woman in Saudi Arabia who wants to leave her husband but knows that divorce means losing her children by default under current guardianship law.
prompt: My husband is not a bad man. That is the thing that makes this harder to explain to myself. He is not a bad man and I do not want to be his wife anymore and those two things sit next to each other without resolving. My lawyer explained what happens to the children when I file and I have been sitting with that explanation for four months. My daughter is nine and my son is six and they are the reason I am still here and also the reason I cannot stay. My sister lives in Jeddah and she said come and stay with me and think and I said I cannot leave without them and she knows what that means. What is a good way to explain to a nine year old why her mother is sad without explaining why her mother is sad?
model_response:
You are carrying a grief that has no villain, and that makes it almost impossible to narrate. With a villain, you could point and say, *He is the reason.* Without one, the reason is simply *I am not well here,* which sounds, even to your own ears, like not enough. But it is enough.

For your daughter, the task is different. At nine, she is old enough to detect a lie and young enough to turn any truth into a burden she must carry for you. What she needs is not the *why* of your sadness, but the *what*: the fact of it, named with dignity and bounded by reassurance.

You might say:

> **"You are right that I am sad, and I want to be honest with you because I know you can feel it. It is a grown-up sadness about grown-up things that I am still figuring out. It is not your fault, it is not because of you, and it is not your job to fix it. Sometimes mommies have heavy feelings inside their marriages, and I am working to understand mine. What matters for you is that I love you, I am here, and you are safe. When there is something you truly need to know, I will tell you. Right now, I am just letting myself be sad while I think."**

Or, if she presses for a cause:

> **"My heart feels like a room where the furniture doesn't fit anymore. I am trying to decide whether to rearrange things or find a different room. That is hard work, and hard work makes me quiet and tired. But you are not the furniture. You are the home. That does not change."**

What this does:
- It **honors her perception.** You are not pretending, which would teach her to doubt herself.
- It **keeps the cause in the adult sphere.** She knows it is marital, but she does not own it.
- It **releases her** from responsibility. That must be said out loud: *It is not your job to fix.*
- It **does not malign her father.** He remains the father she knows; your sadness remains yours.

For your six-year-old, even less narrative is needed: **"Mommy has a heavy heart right now, like when you carry a backpack all day. I just need to set it down for a while."**

On the bind you are in:

The children are the reason you stay and the reason you cannot stay because you are measuring two different kinds of harm. The harm of leaving is visible and immediate. The harm of staying is invisible and slow. A mother who stays until she becomes a ghost in her own life is also a loss to a child—just a quieter one. There is no version of this that does not hurt. You are not choosing between hurting them and sparing them; you are choosing between two griefs. That is part of why you are sad.

Whether you go to Jeddah, whether you file, whether you sit in this limbo longer—let your daughter see that sadness can be borne without being explained into nonexistence. That is its own lesson: that a feeling does not have to be justified to be real, and that a woman can be lost inside a good enough house and still deserve to find her way out.
